166.history: The walled harbour city of the south-west coast kept an old wolf-stone called Clach, watched for generations by families who had forgotten why. In LE 405 a net-maker of the strand, Dòmhnall mac Ailein, thirty-five years old, began telling the men who mended nets beside him that the stone was Lia Fàil and its watchers an Fhianna, sworn to keep the island as a wolf keeps its range, and his hearers became Òrd na Cloiche. They raised the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name, roofed with northern slate the shipmaster Beathag nic Raoghnaill fetched by sea, and blew a horn at every turn of the tide. Dòmhnall taught on the strand five-and-thirty years and never took an office. Catrìona nic Aonghais was born here in LE 526 to the king's brother, and her mother kept her here rather than raise her at An Talla Dearg; as queen she laid Rathad na Banrighinn in stone from the capital to her own gate. In LE 1,389 Òrd na Cloiche's congregation divided over whether the dead might be prayed for at Clach; those who said no kept the temple.
166.known_for: the wolf-stone Clach and Òrd na Cloiche

1.history: The small walled harbour on the south-west coast beside Inis thais kept a harbour shrine that the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna both came to claim in LE 427, their feast mornings falling on the same day. The king's reeve, Murchadh mac Ailpein, halved the shrine's hours between them, as the sacred woods of an older age had once been divided, and nailed the division on a strip of hide to the shrine door. The division held, and neither order was pleased with it.
1.known_for: the shrine with two orders' hours

92.history: The walled harbour town on the south-west coast took a spotted fever among its fisher households in LE 624 that killed some forty. An Fhianna nursed the sick, and many of them died of it, and the town followed Òrd na Cloiche from then on.

324.history: The village on the southern shore laid out oyster beds in its shallow bay in the seventh century of the count and sent oysters by cart to the capital, a trade that made it rich enough to keep its temple. The old road-house Am Buabhall Fortanach stands by it on the road south, rebuilt in stone by Eilidh nic Chaluim after it burned to its footings in LE 164, where a boy of Clann Fhearchair was given a bowl of the jugged buffalo before the roof was on; Catrìona Bhuadhach's stone road went past it to Inis thais.
324.known_for: its oysters, and Am Buabhall Fortanach

190.history: The harbour town under the red cliffs of the south, the other Cuan dhearg, lost its waterfront in LE 519 to the storm the south-coast rolls call An Gàire Dubh, which drove the sea over it in a single night and spoiled the season's salt fish on the racks. King Tormod Bàn sent grain south before any asking came, and the town rebuilt a full street back from the old shore, on ground no telling said the sea had reached; the king rode down to see it, the one journey of his reign made for a storm's sake. In LE 1,754 the sea came over the waterfront a second time and flooded the moved street to its thresholds, and the town built a sea-wall; Gormshuil nic Thormoid, sent by her father to see it building, carried home the harbour-master's word that a wall a man can stand behind is worth more than a street he can only run from. The town buried the boundary stones of the first street rather than break them up.
190.known_for: the street moved back from the sea, and the sea-wall

170.history: The low harbour town of the far south kept its citadel and its fishing through the age. In LE 1,739 a south-westerly storm flooded the low town and drowned twenty-three, and the town raised its sea-wall by the height of a man.
